title: The Caliphate
subtitle: 632–750 · Conquest, the Fitnas and the Umayyad State

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Four elected caliphs at Medina, then a Syrian dynasty that made the office a kingship

entries.label: Abu Bakr and the Ridda
entries.hint: Chosen at the Saqifa gathering over the Prophet's family's claims, Abu Bakr spent his two years holding Arabia together: the tribes that had followed Muhammad now refused Abu Bakr, and the 'wars of apostasy' reconquered the peninsula before the armies turned outward. He nominated Umar to succeed him.
entries.note: The narrative rests almost entirely on al-Tabari (d. 923) and al-Baladhuri (d. 892), compilers working 250+ years later from the akhbar of Sayf ibn Umar (partisan and unreliable), Abu Mikhnaf (pro-Kufan) and al-Waqidi. Contemporary evidence for the 630s is limited to a handful of Greek and Syriac notices (the 'Doctrina Jacobi', c.634) and, from 643, the Arabic papyri.

entries.label: Umar — the conquest state
entries.hint: Umar built the machinery a conquering movement needed: the stipend register (diwan) scaled by precedence in Islam, the garrison cities, the dating of documents from the Hijra, and the title 'Commander of the Faithful'. Syria, Egypt and Iraq were all taken under him. He was stabbed at prayer by a Persian captive in 644.
entries.note: al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri as above; the diwan and land settlement also in Abu Yusuf, 'Kitab al-Kharaj' (d. 798) and Abu Ubayd, 'Kitab al-Amwal' (d. 838) — juristic reconstructions, not archives. The Nessana and Aphrodito papyri give the earliest documentary picture of the new administration.

entries.label: Uthman — the recension and the revolt
entries.hint: Uthman fixed the text of the Quran and staffed the provinces with his Umayyad kin. Grievances over the appointments, the treatment of dissidents and the control of conquered land converged on Medina, where rebels from Egypt and Iraq besieged his house and killed him — the first caliph murdered by Muslims.
entries.note: al-Tabari (drawing here on the lost work of Sayf ibn Umar, which minimises the rebels' grievances, and on al-Waqidi); the pro-Uthman and pro-rebel versions are irreconcilable in the sources. The Quran recension is corroborated by the Sanaa palimpsest and the Birmingham folios (radiocarbon 568–645).

entries.label: Ali — the First Fitna
entries.hint: Ali moved the caliphate to Kufa and fought three wars: against Aisha, Talha and al-Zubayr at the Camel; against Muawiya at Siffin, which ended in an arbitration; and against the Kharijites, who broke from him over that arbitration and killed him at prayer in 661. Shia Islam counts him the first imam.
entries.note: al-Tabari, largely via Abu Mikhnaf (d. 774), a Kufan whose reports are early but sympathetic to the Alid side; the Umayyad-Syrian version is thinner. The Siffin arbitration document is preserved in several recensions (Hinds, JSS 1972) but its authenticity is debated.

entries.label: Muawiya I makes the caliphate a dynasty
entries.hint: Muawiya had governed Syria for twenty years and had a standing army and a treasury. Ruling from Damascus on the Byzantine administrative model, he restored order after the fitna — the sources call 661 'the year of unity' — and then had his son Yazid recognised as heir, the step his critics never forgave.
entries.note: Hawting, 'The First Dynasty of Islam' (2nd ed. 2000). The Umayyad period is written almost entirely by their Abbasid-era enemies; the one substantial contemporary source is documentary — the papyri, the coins, and inscriptions such as the Muawiya dam text near Taif (677/78) and the bath inscription at Hammat Gader.

entries.label: Yazid I, Karbala and the Second Fitna
entries.hint: Yazid's accession was met by Husayn's march on Kufa, which ended in the massacre at Karbala (680), and by the revolt of Medina, crushed with a sack of the city at al-Harra (683). His army then besieged Mecca, where the Kaaba burned. Yazid and his son Muawiya II died within months, and the Sufyanid line ended.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the Karbala narrative descends from Abu Mikhnaf's 'Maqtal al-Husayn', a devotional-political text that shaped Shia liturgy — early but not disinterested. Al-Harra and the Kaaba fire are in the Zubayrid-friendly tradition.

entries.label: Marwan I and the Zubayrid war
entries.loc: Damascus; against Mecca (Ibn al-Zubayr) and Kufa (al-Mukhtar)
entries.hint: With the Sufyanids gone, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr was acknowledged caliph across most of the empire from Mecca. The Syrian tribes chose Marwan of the other Umayyad branch, who won the Battle of Marj Rahit (684). His son then had to reconquer Iraq — from al-Mukhtar's pro-Alid Kufan regime and from the Zubayrids — before the empire was whole again.
entries.note: Rotter, 'Die Umayyaden und der zweite Bürgerkrieg' (1982); al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri. Ibn al-Zubayr's coins survive, giving a rare Umayyad-era documentary check on a contested reign.

entries.label: Abd al-Malik refounds the state
entries.hint: After al-Hajjaj's siege killed Ibn al-Zubayr at Mecca in 692, Abd al-Malik rebuilt: an Arabic-language bureaucracy, a reformed aniconic gold and silver coinage, the Dome of the Rock, and al-Hajjaj installed as viceroy of the whole east. The empire took a form it kept for centuries.
entries.note: Robinson, 'Abd al-Malik' (2005). This reign is unusually well documented in physical evidence: the dated Dome of the Rock inscription (72 AH / 691–92), the coinage sequence, and the switch of the Egyptian papyrus protocol to Arabic.

entries.label: Al-Walid I — the conquests at their limit
entries.hint: Under al-Walid, three fronts advanced at once: Tariq ibn Ziyad destroyed the Visigothic kingdom of Spain (711), Muhammad ibn al-Qasim took Sind (711), and Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered the Sogdian cities of Transoxiana. Al-Walid also built the Great Mosque of Damascus. It was the widest the empire ever reached under one campaign generation.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri; for Sind the later Persian 'Chachnama'. The Damascus mosque is dated by its own foundation inscription and by al-Muqaddasi's 10th-century description; the Barada mosaic panel is in situ.

entries.label: Sulayman, Umar II and Yazid II
entries.hint: Sulayman staked everything on the second siege of Constantinople (717–718) and lost. His successor Umar II, the one Umayyad his enemies praised, tried to fix the tax injustice done to non-Arab converts and to end the ritual cursing of Ali. His early death and the reaction under Yazid II left the problem unsolved.
entries.note: the 'Fiscal Rescript of Umar II' (Gibb, 'Arabica' 1955) survives as a text in the later tradition; its authenticity and scope are disputed. Umar II's near-canonisation in Sunni memory makes his reign the hardest of the period to read straight.

entries.label: Hisham — the long holding operation
entries.loc: the Rusafa, on the Euphrates steppe
entries.hint: Hisham governed for nineteen years from a steppe palace, squeezing revenue, stalling the frontiers and putting down revolt after revolt — Zayd ibn Ali's rising in Kufa (740), the Kharijites, and the great Berber revolt that broke Umayyad North Africa. Historians have called his reign the end of the 'jihad state', the moment expansion stopped paying for itself.
entries.note: Blankinship, 'The End of the Jihad State: The Reign of Hisham' (1994) — the fullest modern treatment, arguing the fiscal-military model was already failing before the revolution. Sources: al-Tabari; the Rusafa (Sergiopolis) excavated.

entries.label: The Third Fitna and the fall of the Umayyads
entries.loc: Syria; Iraq; Harran; the river Zab
entries.hint: Al-Walid II was murdered by his own family in 744, and the Syrian army destroyed itself in a Qays–Yaman civil war under three caliphs in two years. Marwan II moved the capital to Harran and held on until Abu Muslim's Khurasani army, marching under black banners for 'the family of the Prophet', beat him at the Zab in 750 and hunted him down in Egypt.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Sharon, 'Black Banners from the East' (1983) and 'Revolt: The Social and Military Aspects of the Abbasid Revolution' (1990); Agha, 'The Revolution which Toppled the Umayyads' (2003), which stresses the Khurasani-Arab rather than mawali character of the movement.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The conquests, the two great sieges of Constantinople, and the civil wars that made the sects

entries.label: The wars of apostasy
entries.hint: On the Prophet's death much of Arabia repudiated Medina's authority, some following rival prophets — Musaylima in Yamama, Tulayha, the prophetess Sajah. Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaigns, above all the bloody Battle of Yamama, reconquered the peninsula in a year and turned a coalition of tribes back into a state.
entries.note: al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri, drawing on Sayf ibn Umar, whose Ridda narrative is the most detailed and the least trustworthy in the corpus (Donner, 'Narratives of Islamic Origins', 1998). The scale and even the framing of the 'apostasy' are debated.

entries.label: Ajnadayn and Yarmuk — Byzantine Syria falls
entries.hint: Two battles broke Byzantine Syria: Ajnadayn in 634 and, decisively, the six-day fight on the Yarmuk in 636, where a Byzantine field army was destroyed against the river gorges. Heraclius withdrew behind the Taurus, reportedly with the farewell 'Peace to you, Syria'.
entries.note: Kaegi, 'Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests' (1992), reconstructs the campaign critically against al-Tabari, al-Baladhuri and the Syriac chronicles (the 'Chronicle of 1234', dependent on the lost work of Theophilus of Edessa).

entries.label: al-Qadisiyya, Jalula and Nihawand — the end of Sasanian Persia
entries.hint: Al-Hira surrendered on the road; al-Qadisiyya (636) opened Ctesiphon and the Sawad; Jalula and then Nihawand (642), 'the Victory of Victories', broke the last imperial army. The Persian court fled east until Yazdegerd III was murdered near Merv in 651.
entries.note: al-Tabari's Iraq narrative is mostly Sayf ibn Umar's, with its inflated numbers and invented units; the bare outcomes are secure, the details are not. Pourshariati, 'Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire' (2008), argues the Parthian noble houses' defection was decisive.

entries.label: The conquest of Egypt
entries.hint: Amr ibn al-As took Egypt with a small force against little Byzantine resistance: the fortress of Babylon fell in 641, Alexandria was surrendered by treaty in 642, and the garrison town of Fustat — the nucleus of Cairo — was founded beside the Nile. Egypt's grain now fed Arabia by canal and sea.
entries.note: the near-contemporary Coptic 'Chronicle of John of Nikiu' (survives only in a Ge'ez translation) is the best source; al-Baladhuri and the papyri (the Aphrodito archive of governor Qurra ibn Sharik, 709–714) fill in the administration. The 'burning of the Library of Alexandria' story is a 13th-century invention.

entries.label: The Battle of the Camel and Siffin
entries.loc: Basra (the Camel); Siffin, on the upper Euphrates
entries.hint: The first war among Muslims: Ali defeated Aisha, Talha and al-Zubayr outside Basra in a battle named for the camel Aisha rode, then fought Muawiya to a standstill at Siffin. The agreement to submit the dispute to arbitrators split Ali's own army and created the Kharijites.
entries.note: Nasr ibn Muzahim al-Minqari's 'Waq'at Siffin' (d. 827) is the earliest connected account — Kufan and pro-Alid. al-Tabari supplements it. The number and even the fact of the arbitration's terms are contested in the tradition.

entries.label: Karbala
entries.hint: Invited to Kufa and then abandoned by it, Husayn ibn Ali was surrounded by an Umayfad force on the desert plain of Karbala, cut off from the Euphrates, and killed with his male kin and companions; the women and the surviving child were taken to Damascus. The day, Ashura, became the central rite of Shia Islam.
entries.note: the account descends through Abu Mikhnaf's 'Maqtal al-Husayn', preserved in al-Tabari and in later devotional recensions that expanded it steadily. It is early evidence for the event and primary evidence for how the Shia community formed around its memory.

entries.label: al-Harra, the Kaaba fire, and al-Mukhtar
entries.hint: The revolt of Medina ended in 683 with a three-day sack (al-Harra); the Umayyad siege of Mecca that followed left the Kaaba burned by fire from a catapult. In Kufa, al-Mukhtar seized the city in 685 in the name of a son of Ali, hunted down the men responsible for Karbala, and was killed in 687 by the Zubayrids.
entries.note: al-Tabari, from the Kufan and Zubayrid traditions; al-Mukhtar is treated as a fraud by the Sunni sources and a proto-Shia hero by others. The physical damage to the Kaaba is confirmed by the rebuilding that Ibn al-Zubayr and then al-Hajjaj carried out.

entries.label: The first siege of Constantinople
entries.hint: Muawiya's fleets wintered at Cyzicus on the Marmara and pressed the capital for several seasons. The Arabic tradition is thin; the Byzantine account credits the invention of 'Greek fire' by a refugee named Kallinikos with breaking the campaign. The Arabs withdrew and agreed a thirty-year truce.
entries.note: Theophanes (d. 818), whose 7th-century material comes from a lost eastern Christian source (Theophilus of Edessa); Howard-Johnston and Jankowiak have questioned the traditional dating and even the coherence of a single 'siege'.

entries.label: The second siege of Constantinople
entries.hint: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik brought an army and an enormous fleet against the walls in the autumn of 717. A hard winter, a Bulgar attack on the besiegers, defecting Egyptian crews and Greek fire destroyed it; the survivors straggled home in 718. It fixed the northern limit of the first Arab expansion.
entries.note: Theophanes and the 'Chronicle of 819'; the Umayfad court poet al-Farazdaq alludes to the disaster. Modern account: Guilland; Lilie, 'Die byzantinische Reaktion auf die Ausbreitung der Araber' (1976).

entries.label: Transoxiana and the Turgesh war
entries.hint: Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered the Sogdian city-states between 706 and 715, but the tax demands and the fiscal treatment of converts drove repeated revolts. The Turgesh Turkish confederation nearly rolled the Arabs back to the Oxus — the 'Day of Thirst' in 724 was a rout — before Nasr ibn Sayyar stabilised the frontier in the 740s.
entries.note: al-Tabari, largely from al-Mada'ini (d. 843), whose Khurasan reports are relatively sober; Gibb, 'The Arab Conquests in Central Asia' (1923), still the standard narrative. The Sogdian 'Mount Mugh' documents give a rare local-language check.

entries.label: The Great Berber Revolt
entries.loc: the Maghreb; Tangier; the Sebou valley
entries.hint: North African Berbers, most of them Muslim but taxed and enslaved as though they were not, rose under Kharijite banners. They wiped out an Umayyad army at the 'Battle of the Nobles' near Tangier (740) and a second, Syrian, army at the Bagdoura in 741. Umayyad authority never recovered west of Kairouan, and the revolt spilled into Spain.
entries.note: al-Tabari and the later North African compilers (Ibn Idhari, 'al-Bayan al-Mughrib', 13th c.); the Kharijite (Sufri and Ibadi) dimension is best seen through the Ibadi 'siyar' tradition. Cross-references the Al-Andalus 711–1031 folio.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The stipend register, an Arabic bureaucracy, a reformed coinage and the tax of a converting empire

entries.label: The diwan and the garrison cities
entries.hint: Umar registered every Arab fighter and paid an annual stipend (ata) scaled by precedence in Islam, funded from the land tax of the conquered provinces. The soldiers were kept in new garrison towns — Kufa, Basra, Fustat — which became the great cities of Islam and the seedbeds of its law and sects.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri, 'Futuh al-Buldan'; Puin's work on the diwan; the amsar as institutions (Kennedy 2016).

entries.label: Abd al-Malik Arabises the bureaucracy
entries.hint: The tax registers, kept until now in Greek in Syria and Egypt and in Persian in Iraq, were translated into Arabic. Combined with the new coinage it made Arabic the language of the state everywhere — the single most consequential administrative act of the period.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri; al-Jahshiyari, 'Kitab al-Wuzara wa'l-Kuttab'; Robinson, 'Abd al-Malik' (2005).

entries.label: The reformed dinar and dirham
entries.hint: After brief experiments with a 'standing caliph' image, Abd al-Malik issued a purely epigraphic gold dinar and silver dirham carrying Quranic text and no picture. It was the first entirely new imperial currency since Rome, and it announced a state that would not borrow Byzantium's images.
entries.note: the Umayyad coinage reform (Album, 'Checklist of Islamic Coins'; Bacharach; Treadwell on the transitional issues).

entries.label: The fiscal problem of conversion — Umar II's rescript
entries.loc: the empire, esp. Khurasan and Egypt
entries.hint: A convert was still liable for the land tax (kharaj) on his fields, so mass conversion threatened the revenue and the state resisted it. Umar II's fiscal rescript tried to separate the land tax from the person and to admit converts to the stipend — a fix that satisfied no one and outlived him only in fragments.
entries.note: the 'Fiscal Rescript of Umar II' (Gibb's classic study, 1955); the mawali grievance (see Lives).

entries.label: The office of qadi and the beginnings of Islamic law
entries.hint: Governors appointed judges (qadis) to settle disputes among Muslims, and their rulings — drawing on the Quran, remembered practice, local custom and their own reasoning — began to harden into the 'living traditions' of each garrison city. This is where Islamic jurisprudence starts.
entries.note: Schacht, 'The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence' (1950); the Umayyad qadis (Waki', 'Akhbar al-Qudat'); Hallaq, 'The Origins and Evolution of Islamic Law' (2005).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The canonical Quran, the sects born in the fitnas, and the first theology

entries.label: The Uthmanic recension of the Quran
entries.loc: Medina; codices sent to Kufa, Basra, Damascus, Fustat
entries.hint: Uthman had an authoritative consonantal text compiled and copies sent to the garrison cities, with variant collections ordered destroyed. Whatever its exact process, this is the moment the Quran becomes a fixed, empire-wide book — confirmed by the early manuscripts (the Birmingham and Sanaa folios).
entries.note: The traditional account is in al-Bukhari's 'Sahih' (compiled c.850s, ~200 years after the event). The strongest evidence is physical: the Sanaa palimpsest (whose erased lower text preserves a non-Uthmanic recension), the Birmingham folios and the Codex Parisino-petropolitanus, radiocarbon-dated to the mid-7th century. Sinai, 'The Qur'an: A Historical-Critical Introduction' (2017), reviews the debate.

entries.label: The First Fitna makes the sects
entries.hint: Out of the war over Ali's caliphate came the three enduring divisions: the Shia (the party of Ali and his house), the Kharijites (rigorists who judged sinful rulers to be unbelievers), and the majority who suspended judgement on the fitna and became the proto-Sunnis.
entries.note: the sectarian historiography (al-Nawbakhti, 'Firaq al-Shia'; al-Ashari, 'Maqalat'); modern synthesis in Crone, 'Medieval Islamic Political Thought' (2004).

entries.label: The Dome of the Rock and the caliph as God's deputy
entries.hint: Abd al-Malik's shrine over the rock carries the earliest dated monumental Quranic inscriptions — texts affirming God's oneness and denying that God has a son, addressed pointedly at Christianity. The Marwanid caliphs styled themselves khalifat Allah, God's deputy on earth, not merely the Prophet's successor.
entries.note: The primary evidence is the building and its mosaic inscription, dated 72 AH (691–92) — the earliest dated monumental Quranic text and a rare fixed point in Umayyad history. Grabar, 'The Shape of the Holy' (1996); Milwright, 'The Dome of the Rock and its Umayyad Mosaic Inscriptions' (2016). The khalifat Allah title is argued from coins, papyri and poetry, not the hostile Abbasid-era prose (Crone & Hinds, 'God's Caliph', 1986).

entries.label: The isnad and the first hadith collectors
entries.hint: As the Companions died, reports of what the Prophet said and did began to be transmitted with a named chain of authorities (isnad). Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri (d. 742), working partly for the Umayyad court, was the first to gather this material systematically — the beginning of the hadith sciences.
entries.note: al-Zuhri left no book; his material survives as quotations in al-Tabari, Ibn Ishaq and the hadith collections. Whether continuous isnad-backed transmission is as old as it claims is the field's central source-critical problem: Schacht (1950) dated it late; Motzki, 'The Origins of Islamic Jurisprudence' (2002), pushed it back toward al-Zuhri's generation with the isnad-cum-matn method.

entries.label: Free will, sin and the community — the first theological disputes
entries.hint: Two questions split the early scholars: is a Muslim who commits a grave sin still a believer (the Murji'a said yes, judgement is God's), and are human acts free or predestined (the Qadariyya insisted on free will, against a fatalism convenient to the Umayyads). These are the seeds of Islamic theology.
entries.note: the 'Risala' attributed to al-Hasan al-Basri on qadar; van Ess, 'Theologie und Gesellschaft im 2. und 3. Jahrhundert Hidschra' vol. 1 (1991).

entries.label: Al-Hasan al-Basri and the beginnings of renunciation
entries.hint: Preacher, jurist, traditionist and ascetic, al-Hasan al-Basri stood at the head of nearly every strand of later Islamic piety. His sermons on fear of God and detachment from the world are the earliest sustained expression of the current that would become Sufism.
entries.note: the sayings of al-Hasan al-Basri (Ritter's studies; Mourad, 'Early Islam between Myth and History', 2006).

entries.label: John of Damascus answers Islam
entries.loc: Mar Saba monastery, near Jerusalem; earlier an Umayyad official
entries.hint: A Christian who had served in the Umayyad tax administration, John of Damascus wrote the first substantial Christian analysis of Islam, treating it as 'the heresy of the Ishmaelites' and supplying arguments Byzantine polemicists used for centuries. The empire's Christian majority was working out how to live under, and argue with, the new order.
entries.note: John of Damascus, 'On Heresies' ch. 100 — a genuinely contemporary insider (he served in the Umayyad fisc before entering Mar Saba c.706), which is rare for this period. Ed. Kotter; Sahas, 'John of Damascus on Islam' (1972); Griffith, 'The Church in the Shadow of the Mosque' (2008). The chapter's attribution to John himself is generally but not universally accepted.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Dome of the Rock, the hypostyle mosque, the desert palaces and the aniconic turn

entries.label: The Dome of the Rock — the first monument of Islamic art
entries.hint: An octagon of Byzantine construction and Sasanian and classical ornament, crowned by a golden dome and sheathed inside in mosaic — but with no human or animal figure and a band of Arabic Quranic text as its central decoration. Islamic architecture announces itself by what it refuses as much as by what it borrows.
entries.note: Grabar, 'The Dome of the Rock' (2006); the building as a statement in the religious landscape of Jerusalem.

entries.label: The Great Mosque of Damascus
entries.hint: Built by al-Walid I on the site of a cathedral that had been a temple of Jupiter, the Damascus mosque fixed the classic form — a broad courtyard, a wide prayer hall on the qibla side, a mihrab niche and minbar — and covered its walls in a mosaic vision of a paradise of rivers and palaces with, again, no living creature in it.
entries.note: the Barada mosaic panel; Flood, 'The Great Mosque of Damascus' (2001).

entries.label: The Umayyad desert palaces
entries.loc: Qusayr Amra, Mshatta, Khirbat al-Mafjar, Qasr al-Hayr
entries.hint: Away from the mosques, the Umayyad princes built fortified pleasure-houses in the Syrian steppe with bath-suites frescoed with hunting scenes, dancing girls, personifications, a zodiac dome and the 'Six Kings of the Earth'. Umayyad secular art was figural, sensuous and squarely in the Late Antique tradition.
entries.note: Qusayr Amra (UNESCO; Fowden, 'Qusayr Amra: Art and the Umayyad Elite in Late Antique Syria', 2004); Khirbat al-Mafjar (Hamilton).

entries.label: The aniconic turn on the coinage
entries.hint: Umayyad mints first tried a caliph in Arab dress holding a sword, then abandoned the human image entirely for pure Arabic script. The choice — figural for the palace, wordless for the coin and the mosque — set a lasting boundary between Islamic sacred and secular art.
entries.note: the transitional 'standing caliph' dinars and their replacement (Treadwell on the transitional 'Orans' drachms; Album).

entries.label: The early Quran manuscripts
entries.hint: The oldest Qurans — the Hijazi script leaning to the right, then the first upright Kufic — were large, sparely pointed, written on parchment in a format meant for display and recitation. They are the founding objects of Arabic calligraphy, the art Islam prized above all others.
entries.note: the Sanaa, Birmingham and Paris-Petropolitanus manuscripts; Déroche, 'Qur'ans of the Umayyads' (2014).

entries.label: The court poets and the first Arab art music
entries.hint: The Umayyad court kept rival panegyrists — Jarir, al-Farazdaq and the Christian al-Akhtal traded verse insults (naqaid) for a generation — while in the Hijaz the love lyric (ghazal) flourished and singers like Ibn Misjah and the mukhannath Tuways set poetry to modal song, founding classical Arabic music.
entries.note: From al-Isfahani's 'Kitab al-Aghani' (d. 967) — a vast anecdotal compilation written ~250 years after the Umayyad Hijaz it describes, rich but not documentary. The naqaid of Jarir and al-Farazdaq survive as an independently transmitted poetic corpus (ed. Bevan, 1905–12).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Exegesis and grammar are born together; law and history begin to be written

entries.label: The beginnings of Quranic exegesis
entries.hint: Explaining the Quran — its occasions of revelation, its obscure words, its legal verses — began with Companions like Ibn Abbas and grew into the discipline of tafsir. The need to make the text intelligible to non-Arab converts drove much of the early effort.
entries.note: the exegetical material attributed to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid (Rippin's studies); the transmission problem (Versteegh, 'Arabic Grammar and Qur'anic Exegesis in Early Islam', 1993).

entries.label: Arabic grammar and the two schools
entries.hint: To fix the correct reading of the Quran for a rapidly non-Arab community, scholars began to codify Arabic — its inflections, its syntax — as a formal science. Basra and Kufa developed rival methods, and the discipline culminated a generation later in Sibawayh's 'Kitab', the grammar of the language.
entries.note: the tradition tracing grammar to Abu al-Aswad al-Duali; the Basra/Kufa schools (Carter; Versteegh, 'The Arabic Language', 1997).

entries.label: The Prophet's biography takes written form
entries.hint: Urwa ibn al-Zubayr began collecting reports of the Prophet's campaigns (maghazi); Ibn Ishaq (d. 767) assembled them, with the pre-Islamic background and the Meccan preaching, into a continuous 'Life' (sira). It is the framework through which the origins of Islam have been told ever since.
entries.note: Ibn Ishaq (d. 767) wrote ~130 years after the events; his 'Sira' survives only in Ibn Hisham's edited recension (d. 833) and in al-Tabari's quotations of a different transmission line. Urwa ibn al-Zubayr's earlier maghazi material is recoverable only as fragments (Schoeler, 'The Biography of Muhammad', 2011).

entries.label: The Kharijite and Shia arguments about legitimate rule
entries.hint: Early Islam's first political theory was made by its dissidents: the Kharijites held that any pious Muslim, 'even an Ethiopian slave', could be imam and that an unjust ruler forfeited his office and his life; the Shia held that authority belonged by God's designation to the Prophet's house. Both defined themselves against the Umayyad fact.
entries.note: Crone, 'Medieval Islamic Political Thought' (2004), chs. 1–3; the Ibadi 'siyar'; early Shia hadith.

entries.label: The first translations and the Marwanid interest in learning
entries.hint: Medical, astrological and administrative texts were turned from Greek and Persian into Arabic under the Umayyads, and the prince Khalid ibn Yazid was remembered as a patron of alchemy. The great translation movement of the Abbasids had Umayyad beginnings.
entries.note: the Umayyad-era translations (Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture', 1998, ch. 1); the Khalid ibn Yazid legend and its kernel.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: From plunder to a tax state — one currency, one market, from the Atlantic to the Indus

entries.label: The conquest economy — booty, the fifth and the fay'
entries.hint: The first decades ran on plunder: movable spoil was divided among the fighters after the state's fifth (khums), while conquered land was mostly kept intact as fay', its taxes funding the stipend register. War paid for the state, and the state paid the warriors.
entries.note: Abu Ubayd, 'Kitab al-Amwal'; Donner, 'The Early Islamic Conquests' (1981), ch. 5.

entries.label: One market from the Atlantic to the Indus
entries.loc: the Mediterranean, the Red Sea, the Gulf, the Silk Road
entries.hint: For the first time since antiquity a single authority held the whole land bridge between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, and the old Roman–Persian frontier that had taxed and blocked east–west trade was gone. Goods, coins and people moved across it under one law and one currency.
entries.note: the 'Pirenne thesis' debate on Mediterranean unity (McCormick, 'Origins of the European Economy', 2001); the removal of the imperial frontier.

entries.label: The crop transfers begin
entries.loc: Iraq, Iran, Egypt, then the Mediterranean
entries.hint: Sugar cane, rice, cotton, citrus, bananas, aubergines and hard wheat began spreading west out of India and Iran across the unified empire, along with the irrigation and crop-rotation techniques to grow them. It reshaped the agriculture and diet of half the world over the following centuries.
entries.note: Watson, 'Agricultural Innovation in the Early Islamic World' (1983) — the thesis and its critics (Decker, 2009).

entries.label: Al-Hajjaj and the reclamation of lower Iraq
entries.loc: the Sawad; the new city of Wasit
entries.hint: Abd al-Malik's governor al-Hajjaj drove a programme of canal-digging and marsh drainage in southern Iraq to raise the land revenue, founding the garrison-and-administration city of Wasit midway between Kufa and Basra. The reclamation used large gangs of imported East African labour.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri on al-Hajjaj's canals; the labour regime that seeded the later Zanj revolt (Popovic, 'The Revolt of African Slaves in Iraq', 1999).

entries.label: Mecca becomes a pilgrimage economy
entries.hint: Stripped of political power when the capital moved to Damascus, the Hijaz cities were rebuilt as places of pilgrimage and leisure — subsidised grain, a paved road from Iraq (the Darb Zubayda came later), and an economy of hostels, guides and the luxury trades serving pilgrims and the Medinan singing salons.
entries.note: the Hijaz under the Umayyads (Munt, 'The Holy City of Medina', 2014); the pilgrimage infrastructure.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The relay post, the papyrus chancery, and the fleet that contested the sea

entries.label: The barid — the imperial relay
entries.hint: Abd al-Malik systematised the barid, a network of post-stations with fresh mounts carrying official mail and, above all, intelligence to the caliph. Adapted from Roman and Persian models, it was the nervous system that let one court in Damascus govern from Spain to Sind.
entries.note: al-Jahshiyari; Silverstein, 'Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World' (2007).

entries.label: Papyrus, the chancery and the 'protocol'
entries.hint: Egypt's state papyrus workshops supplied the whole empire's administration. Each roll opened with a printed header (protokollon) naming the caliph and the standard — first in Greek, from Abd al-Malik's time in Arabic — the origin of the word 'protocol' and of a vast documentary record now recovered from the sands.
entries.note: One of the few well-documented areas: the Greek, Coptic and Arabic papyri of Egypt — the Aphrodito archive of governor Qurra ibn Sharik (709–714), the Nessana papyri — show the administration working and its language shifting to Arabic under Abd al-Malik. Sijpesteijn, 'Shaping a Muslim State' (2013).

entries.label: The Arab fleet and the Battle of the Masts
entries.hint: Muawiya, as governor of Syria, built ships and crews from the coastal population and in 655 destroyed a Byzantine fleet at the 'Battle of the Masts' off Anatolia. Command of the eastern Mediterranean was now contested, and the sieges of Constantinople became possible.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri; Theophanes; the early Arab navy (Fahmy, 'Muslim Naval Organisation'; Christides).

entries.label: Water engineering across the empire
entries.loc: Iraq (canals), the Hijaz (Mecca's wells and dams), Iran, Spain
entries.hint: The unified state maintained and extended the hydraulic works it inherited — the canal grid of Iraq, the qanats of Iran, Roman aqueducts in Syria and Spain — and moved techniques between provinces. Umayyad dams above Mecca and Taif still stand.
entries.note: the Umayyad dams of the Hijaz (Miles); the maintenance of the Iraqi canal system (Christensen, 'The Decline of Iranshahr', 1993).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The old frontier gone: Byzantium as enemy-partner, India and the Turk world reached, an embassy to China

entries.label: Byzantium — the enemy who lent the mosaicists
entries.hint: Umayyad–Byzantine relations were a routine of raids, tribute payments, prisoner exchanges and, remarkably, cultural loans: Byzantine emperors sent craftsmen and mosaic cubes for the mosques of Damascus and Medina. The two empires fought along a fixed line and did business across it.
entries.note: The mosaicist loans rest on the Arabic sources (al-Tabari; later al-Muqaddasi on Damascus) and are plausible but not independently confirmed; the truces and tribute are in Theophanes. El-Cheikh, 'Byzantium Viewed by the Arabs' (2004).

entries.label: The eastern conquests — Sind and Transoxiana
entries.hint: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim took Sind and the lower Indus in 711; Qutayba ibn Muslim took the Sogdian cities of Transoxiana in the same years. The empire now touched India directly and bordered the Turkish steppe — contacts that would shape its science, its slave armies and its trade.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri; the 'Chachnama' for Sind; Gibb, 'The Arab Conquests in Central Asia' (1923).

entries.label: An inherited bureaucracy — Greek, Coptic and Persian officials
entries.hint: For two generations the empire was run by the same Greek, Coptic and Persian secretaries who had run it before, keeping the accounts in their own languages and scripts. The administrative knowledge of two fallen empires passed intact into the third before it was translated.
entries.note: the papyrological evidence (Sijpesteijn 2013); John of Damascus's family as a case (the Mansur clan of Damascus tax officials).

entries.label: The first Arab embassy to Tang China
entries.hint: Chinese records note an envoy from the 'Dashi' (the Arabs) reaching the Tang court in 651, the year Yazdegerd III died at Merv. The two largest empires on Earth had become neighbours across Central Asia, and the road between them was now open end to end.
entries.note: the 'Jiu Tang shu' and 'Xin Tang shu' notices; the run-up to the Battle of Talas (751).

entries.label: Iberia and the far west
entries.hint: Tariq ibn Ziyad's Berber-led army destroyed the Visigothic kingdom in 711 and within a decade Muslim raiders were north of the Pyrenees. The Umayyad west reached its high-water mark near Tours in 732; thereafter the frontier settled on the Ebro and the Pyrenees.
entries.note: the Arabic and Latin sources on 711 (Collins, 'The Arab Conquest of Spain 710–797', 1989); cross-references the Al-Andalus 711–1031 folio.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: One empire replaces two — Persia gone, Byzantium halved, and a revolution out of the east

entries.label: The Sassanid Empire falls
entries.loc: Iran; the last court at Merv
entries.hint: The Persian Empire that had faced Rome for seven centuries collapsed in under twenty years. Its dynasty ended with Yazdegerd III's murder, but its bureaucrats, its court culture, its titles and its ideas of kingship were absorbed by the caliphate and shaped it permanently.
entries.note: Pourshariati, 'Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire' (2008); the Persian inheritance of the caliphate (see the Abbasid folio).

entries.label: Byzantium survives, transformed
entries.hint: Shorn of Syria, Egypt and Africa — two-thirds of its territory and most of its revenue — the eastern Roman state contracted onto the Anatolian plateau, reorganised its army into land-holding regional 'themes', and became the medieval Byzantium: smaller, poorer, Greek, and permanently on the defensive.
entries.note: Haldon, 'Byzantium in the Seventh Century' (1990); the theme system as a survival mechanism.

entries.label: The limits fixed — Constantinople 718, Tours 732, Talas 751
entries.loc: the Bosphorus; Aquitaine; the Talas river
entries.hint: Three checks a generation apart marked the edges of the first expansion: the failed siege of Constantinople in 718, the turning-back of a raid near Tours in 732, and the clash with Tang China at Talas in 751. Later writers made these into the salvation of civilisations; at the time they were the ordinary friction of an over-extended frontier.
entries.note: on the inflation of Tours' significance (Bachrach); the actual strategic picture (Blankinship, 'The End of the Jihad State', 1994).

entries.label: Qays and Yaman — the faction that ran the empire
entries.hint: Umayyad politics ran on a split between two blocs of Arab tribes, 'northern' Qays and 'southern' Yaman, that cut across every province and every army. Which bloc a governor favoured decided careers, revolts and the loyalty of garrisons — and the feud helped bring the dynasty down.
entries.note: Crone, 'Tribes and States in the Middle East', JRAS (1993); the factional structure of Umayyad government (Hawting 2000).

entries.label: The Abbasid Revolution
entries.hint: A movement organising for decades in the name of 'the family of the Prophet' rose in Khurasan under Abu Muslim, took Kufa, and defeated the last Umayyad army at the Zab. Power passed to the Abbasid line, the centre of the empire moved from Syria to Iraq, and the mawali grievance was, for a moment, answered.
entries.note: Sharon, 'Black Banners from the East' (1983) and 'Revolt' (1990); Agha, 'The Revolution which Toppled the Umayyads' (2003). Continued in the next folio.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The converts who were not equal, the women of the first generation, and the enslaved musicians who made the music

entries.label: The mawali — Muslims of the second rank
entries.loc: the garrison cities; Khurasan; North Africa
entries.hint: A non-Arab who converted became a mawla — a client attached to an Arab tribe, expected to keep paying the taxes of a non-Muslim and excluded from the full military stipend. Islam preached equality; the Umayyad state ran on Arab privilege. The contradiction armed the revolution that destroyed it.
entries.note: the mawali institution (Crone, 'Roman, Provincial and Islamic Law', 1987, on wala'); the grievance in the Abbasid movement (Sharon 1983).

entries.label: The women of the first generation
entries.hint: Aisha bint Abi Bakr led an army against Ali at the Battle of the Camel in 656, then spent forty years as a leading authority on hadith and law. Other women of the Companions' families held property, ran businesses, transmitted traditions and, like Sukayna bint al-Husayn in Medina, presided over literary salons.
entries.note: Spellberg, 'Politics, Gender, and the Islamic Past: The Legacy of Aisha bint Abi Bakr' (1994); Sayeed, 'Women and the Transmission of Religious Knowledge in Islam' (2013).

entries.label: The mukhannathun and the qiyan — the makers of Arab music
entries.hint: Classical Arabic music was created in the Umayyad Hijaz largely by two groups on the social margin: the qiyan, trained singing-girls who were usually enslaved, and the mukhannathun, gender-variant men — Tuways, al-Dalal, Ibn Surayj — who dressed and behaved as women and dominated the profession. Both were periodically persecuted by caliphs who enjoyed their art.
entries.note: Kitab al-Aghani; Rowson, 'The Effeminates of Early Medina', JAOS 111 (1991); the persecution and castration orders under the later Umayyads. Cross-references the pre-Islamic mukhannath entries.

entries.label: The conquest slave supply and the umm walad
entries.hint: Conquest and raiding fed a huge slave trade — captives from Anatolia, the Berber lands, Central Asia and East Africa working as soldiers, farm gangs, domestics and concubines. Law gave one group a route out: a slave woman who bore her master a child became an umm walad, could not be sold, and was freed at his death, her child free and legitimate.
entries.note: the umm walad in early fiqh (Schacht); the slave supply of the conquests (Gordon, 'The Breaking of a Thousand Swords', 2001, for the military side).

entries.label: The dhimmis — the protected majority
entries.hint: For a century the empire's population was overwhelmingly Christian, Jewish and Zoroastrian, living under the 'protection' (dhimma) of the Muslim state: free to worship and self-govern, liable for the poll tax (jizya), and subject to a growing body of restrictions later codified as the 'Pact of Umar'. The churches and the Jewish exilarchate carried on much as before.
entries.note: the 'Pact of Umar' as a later text projected back (Levy-Rubin, 'Non-Muslims in the Early Islamic Empire', 2011); the continuity of the eastern churches (Griffith 2008).
